thesis.question: How can teams sustain AI-assisted development when the architecture changes faster than people can understand and own it?
thesis.claim: Teams should stabilize domain boundaries, API contracts, and data models while allowing fast changes within them, because continuous re-architecting destroys shared ownership and concentrates validation work on a few engineers.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that repeated end-to-end regeneration and enough after-the-fact testing can sustain rapid development without deliberately holding architectural boundaries stable.
thesis.so_what: Architecture decisions determine whether increased output can scale across teams without exhausting the people who understand the system.
thesis.how_why: When boundaries keep moving, local reasoning and durable ownership fail; the few people able to follow the whole system inherit the coordination and validation burden, while stable seams make that work divisible.

supporting_claims.claim: Generated changes can outrun shared understanding, and brute-force generation plus after-the-fact verification consumes finite technical and human capacity.
Continuous re-architecting produces a distinct temporal failure: a system can look modular today while its moving foundations prevent safe local reasoning over time.
Moving boundaries create avoidable cognitive load and concentrate ownership and validation on the few engineers who can still understand the whole system.
Whole-system understanding can sustain a small team's speed, but it cannot replace the durable boundaries a larger organization needs to coordinate.
Deliberately controlling changes to domain boundaries, API contracts and data models makes ownership divisible while preserving fast change within those seams.

role.contribution: Shows how architecture can protect and distribute the understanding that the preceding essay says people must retain.

flow.rationale: Begin with an unreviewable change and the trust gap, then show why more generation and verification effort is unsustainable. Name continuous re-architecting and distinguish the temporal monolith before deriving cognitive load, concentrated ownership and the scaling limit. Only then can stable seams answer a specific failure rather than become generic governance advice. Put Monday actions and the preserved reflection questions before the final synthesis and platform hand-off. Moving the human cost after the solution would turn a co-equal part of the thesis into an aside; moving the taxonomy after it would leave the causal mechanism undefined.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Trust and sustainability are the scarce resources that frame the architecture problem in AI-assisted development.

evidence.what:
> **KEY POINTS:**
>
> * **Software now grows faster than our trust in it.** AI lets us generate code by brute force and verify it by brute force — and brute force burns hardware, money, tokens, and, most of all, the engineers who are *best* at AI. That gap, not raw capability, is the problem.
> * The architectural symptom is **continuous re-architecting**, and its product is the **Vibe Monolith**: a system that is modular on paper yet behaves as one rigid entity, because its foundations never hold still long enough for anyone to own or reason about a single part.
> * Architecture's job now is to **cool the system down** — freeze the highest-blast-radius seams (**domain boundaries, API contracts, the data model**) and let AI move fast inside them. **The way out of the burn is not more force; it is better structure.**

conclusion.heading: Closing Thought
conclusion.synthesis: Trust, maintainability and human sustainability meet in the same architectural decision: a team can sustain generated output only when the boundaries make understanding and responsibility shareable.
conclusion.so_what: Choosing what must remain stable limits how much validation falls on the few people who understand the whole system, allowing speed to persist beyond a small group.

non_goals.topic: Not a verdict that AI-assisted development is bad or should be slowed; the fix is governance that matches the speed, not slower generation.
Not a tools comparison or a how-to for any specific agent, framework, or platform.
Not a microservices-vs-monolith debate; the Vibe Monolith can occur *inside* a clean microservice architecture.
Not a burnout self-help piece; the burnout is framed as a structural consequence of architectural instability, not an individual failing.
The people cost does not get reduced to a mere symptom of the architecture problem, nor the architecture problem to a mere cause of burnout — the two halves close a loop; keep both first-class.
